content.text: When electric current flows through a conductor, it does not flow without opposition. The conductor resists the flow of charge to some extent. This opposition to current flow is called
. Understanding resistance is essential for designing circuits, selecting appropriate components, and predicting how circuits will behave.

In this lesson, we will define resistance, explore Ohm's law, examine the current-voltage characteristics of different components, and investigate the factors that affect the resistance of a conductor.

When free electrons drift through a metallic conductor, they collide with the vibrating metal ions in the crystal lattice. These collisions impede the flow of electrons and transfer kinetic energy from the electrons to the ions, causing the conductor to heat up. This opposition to electron flow is what we call resistance.

Materials with more free electrons and a more orderly lattice structure tend to have lower resistance. Materials with fewer free electrons or more lattice imperfections tend to have higher resistance.
The current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, provided the temperature (and other physical conditions) remain constant.

(forward bias): No current flows until the potential difference reaches a certain threshold (about 0.6-0.7 V for a silicon diode). Above this threshold, the current increases rapidly with a small increase in voltage. The resistance is very low in forward bias above the threshold.
(reverse bias): Virtually no current flows. The resistance is extremely high. The diode effectively blocks the current.

Record pairs of current and voltage readings.

The resistance of a metallic conductor depends on four factors:
to the length of the conductor:
If you double the length of a wire, you double its resistance. This is because the electrons have to travel through more of the material, encountering more collisions with metal ions along the way.
to the cross-sectional area of the conductor:

If you double the cross-sectional area (use a thicker wire), the resistance halves. A thicker wire provides more "lanes" for the electrons to flow through, just as a wider road allows more traffic to flow.

"A diode has infinite resistance in reverse bias."

While the resistance in reverse bias is extremely high, it is not truly infinite. A very small leakage current flows. Also, if the reverse voltage exceeds the breakdown voltage, a large reverse current can flow, which may damage the diode.

Explain why the resistance of a filament lamp increases as current increases.

As the current through the filament increases, more electrical energy is converted to heat, raising the temperature of the tungsten filament. At higher temperatures, the metal ions in the lattice vibrate with greater amplitude. This increases the frequency of collisions between the drifting free electrons and the vibrating ions, which opposes the flow of electrons more strongly. Therefore, the resistance increases.
